headline_en: UAE and UK are now the main sources of remittance; why?
summary_en: In the first eight months of FY2023-24 (July to February) the UAE and the UK overtook Saudi Arabia and the United States as Bangladesh's top remittance sources, per Bangladesh Bank data. Bankers credit better rates and incentives for formal transfers; analysts suspect some laundered money in Dubai is being routed back as remittance to collect the incentive. RMMRU's Tasneem Siddiqui says Saudi remittances fell because of hundi and because many workers who recently went to Saudi Arabia on valid visas found no jobs and came back.

facts.statement: In the first eight months of FY2023-24 (July to February) the largest remittance to Bangladesh came from the United Arab Emirates, followed by the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, the United States and Italy.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank data cited by the reporter

facts.statement: In the two fiscal years before FY2023-24, Saudi Arabia was first and the United States second as remittance sources for Bangladesh, with the UAE third and the UK fourth.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

facts.statement: Bangladesh received a total of USD 1,508 crore in remittance from July to February of FY2023-24: about USD 291 crore from the UAE, about USD 188 crore from the UK, USD 179 crore from Saudi Arabia, USD 168 crore from the United States and about USD 100 crore from Italy; these five countries made up about 61 percent of the eight-month total.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank latest updated data

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh from the UAE was about USD 207 crore in FY2021-22, about USD 303 crore in FY2022-23, and about USD 291 crore in just the first eight months of FY2023-24, an average of USD 36 crore 32 lakh a month; at that average another USD 145 crore could come in the remaining four months, taking the FY2023-24 total above USD 435 crore.
facts.source_in_article: reporter, from Bangladesh Bank data

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh from the UK was about USD 204 crore and about USD 208 crore in the previous two fiscal years, and about USD 188 crore in the first eight months of FY2023-24; at the current monthly average it could exceed USD 250 crore by the end of the fiscal year.
facts.source_in_article: reporter, from Bangladesh Bank data

facts.statement: Remittance from Saudi Arabia has been falling for more than a year and a half: USD 454 crore in FY2021-22 (when Saudi Arabia was the top source), USD 376 crore in FY2022-23, and about USD 179 crore in the first eight months of FY2023-24; people in the sector expect the FY2023-24 total to stay below USD 300 crore.
facts.source_in_article: reporter, from Bangladesh Bank data; sector people

facts.statement: Remittance from the United States was about USD 344 crore in FY2021-22, USD 352 crore in FY2022-23 and about USD 168 crore in the first eight months of FY2023-24; if the trend continues the year-end figure may be around USD 250 crore.
facts.source_in_article: reporter, from Bangladesh Bank data

facts.statement: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU, said many migrant workers who recently went to Saudi Arabia on valid visas are not getting jobs, and many of them are returning to Bangladesh without work; she gave this as one reason remittance from Saudi Arabia has fallen.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair, Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU)

facts.statement: Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said many expatriates are sending money through hundi because of the exchange-rate difference and a lack of trust in banks.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, RMMRU

facts.statement: Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said money sent from the United States to Bangladesh rose abnormally over the previous two years out of fear that the US might impose sanctions on Bangladesh, and has fallen again now that the fear has passed.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, RMMRU

facts.statement: For remittances the official dollar rate at banks is BDT 110; on top of that the government gives a 2.5 percent incentive per dollar and various banks give an equal amount of incentive, so expatriates sending money through legal channels get more than BDT 115 per dollar. Because of the dollar shortage some banks are buying remittance at more than BDT 120.
facts.source_in_article: people in the sector, to the reporter

facts.statement: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director of Mutual Trust Bank, said expatriates now get good benefits for sending money through legal channels, banks are encouraging them in various ways, and a lot of promotion was done in the UAE in particular, which is why remittance from the UAE rose.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director, Mutual Trust Bank

facts.statement: Analysts say Dubai has become a favourite destination of Bangladesh's rich, entrepreneurs and political figures and Bangladeshi businesses there are growing; some suspect part of the money laundered from Bangladesh to Dubai is being brought back as remittance to collect the incentive and is then laundered out again illegally, which would explain the sudden rise in legal-channel remittance from the UAE.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed analysts

facts.statement: A top executive of a bank, speaking anonymously, said many Bangladeshis have built huge assets in the UAE with laundered money and that through some banks part of that money is coming back in the name of remittance to take the incentive.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed top executive of a bank

facts.statement: Former Bangladesh Bank governor Mohammed Farashuddin said at a BIBM event in Mirpur, Dhaka, that a large part of the government's remittance incentive is going to 'big fish' and middlemen, who give part of the incentive to the people sending remittance and keep the rest while bringing money in through illicit routes.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammed Farashuddin, former governor, Bangladesh Bank

headline_en: Seven challenges facing the new foreign minister in a difficult time
summary_en: A column by former foreign secretary Md. Touhid Hossain lists seven diplomatic challenges for new foreign minister Hasan Mahmud after the January 2024 election: relations with the US, EU, UK, India, the India-China balance, Myanmar and the Rohingya, and human rights. Migration appears only briefly: US remittance of USD 352 crore in FY2022-23, and a closing note that the overseas labour market and human trafficking, though under other ministries, end up as problems the foreign ministry must handle.

facts.statement: Remittance of USD 352 crore came to Bangladesh from the United States in FY2022-23, placing the US right after Saudi Arabia as a remittance source.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain, former foreign secretary

facts.statement: Former foreign secretary Md. Touhid Hossain wrote that the overseas labour market has its own ministry, but the task of handling the irregularities and problems that arise in it falls on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; human trafficking is a Ministry of Home Affairs matter, yet the foreign minister will also come under pressure over it at various times.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain, former foreign secretary

facts.statement: The United States announced a visa restriction policy in May 2023 for officials of the administration, law enforcement, politicians and even the judiciary who would obstruct a fair election in Bangladesh, and said the restriction took effect from 22 September 2023.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain

facts.statement: The columnist notes that the Rohingya camps have become a centre of armed conflict, drugs and human trafficking, and that no progress was made in five years on returning more than 10 lakh Rohingya refugees.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain

facts.statement: The columnist notes that the UK is the third largest destination for Bangladeshi export goods and that a huge Bangladeshi community lives there.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Md. Touhid Hossain

headline_en: Migrant workers get insurance money easily only when they die abroad
summary_en: The article explains the compulsory 'Probashi Kormi Bima' (expatriate worker insurance) run by the Wage Earners' Welfare Board with Jiban Bima Corporation: who is covered, what it pays, what it excludes, and how few claims are made. Death payouts reach the family's bank account without an application, but disability and early-return benefits must be claimed and most workers do not know the insurance exists. Families of workers whose foreign death certificate says 'suicide' get no insurance, and rights groups want suicide, HIV/AIDS deaths and health cover included.

facts.statement: The government introduced compulsory 'Probashi Kormi Bima' (expatriate worker insurance) for Bangladeshi workers going abroad at the end of 2019. The Wage Earners' Welfare Board, under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, signed the agreement with the state-owned Jiban Bima Corporation on 12 December 2019 and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina inaugurated it on 19 December 2019; the initial insurance term was two years.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

facts.statement: A new expatriate worker insurance agreement was signed on 12 March 2023 setting the sum insured at BDT 10 lakh; workers aged 18 to 55 going abroad are covered for five years, counted from the date they receive emigration clearance (bohirgomon chharpotro).
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: Under the new expatriate worker insurance agreement, benefits are payable within the insurance term for the worker's death, permanent disability, partial permanent disability, or if the worker loses the job and returns to Bangladesh within six months.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: If a worker dies of natural causes or by accident during the insurance term or within 90 days after it expires, the full insured sum of BDT 10 lakh is paid.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: A worker who is dismissed and returns to Bangladesh within six months gets BDT 50,000 under the expatriate worker insurance; this benefit does not apply if the worker went abroad entirely at the employer's cost.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: The expatriate worker insurance does not pay if the worker dies by suicide or self-harm within six months of the insurer taking on the risk; for death or illness from HIV/AIDS or similar diseases; for death in risky sports or adventurous activities (motor racing, boxing, scuba diving, horse racing, mountain climbing and others); for death due to alcohol or drug addiction; for death in war or riot or by an attack by miscreants; or for a worker executed under a court sentence.
facts.source_in_article: the new agreement, cited by the reporter

facts.statement: A worker going abroad has to pay the applicable insurance premium together with the other fees paid for emigration clearance; the article does not state the premium amount.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

facts.statement: When a worker dies abroad, no application is needed for the insurance after the body arrives in Bangladesh: the insurance money is deposited in the dead worker's bank account. In other cases (disability, early return) the insurance has to be claimed.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation sources

facts.statement: By Jiban Bima Corporation's count, 3,224,343 workers went to various countries for work from the start of the insurance to the end of 2023, and in that time 1,397 workers or their family members claimed insurance money.
facts.source_in_article: Jiban Bima Corporation

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board's 2022-23 annual report says 1,125,836 workers came under the compulsory insurance in that fiscal year, and the families of 860 workers were paid BDT 31 crore 72 lakh 10 thousand as death insurance.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board annual report 2022-23

facts.statement: Government bodies have no information on workers who return with a disability or who come back within six months, the Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation sources said; claims other than for death abroad have not risen much.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board and Jiban Bima Corporation sources

facts.statement: Although the insurance is compulsory, people concerned say there is no special effort to inform workers about it before they go abroad; many workers do not know the process, the rules for getting the money or the policy, and so miss out.
facts.source_in_article: people concerned, to the reporter

facts.statement: Md. Mosharraf Hossain, manager of expatriate worker insurance at Jiban Bima Corporation, said meetings have been held on how to make workers aware of the insurance before they leave and emphasis is being put on telling workers about it during various trainings.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Mosharraf Hossain, manager, expatriate worker insurance, Jiban Bima Corporation

facts.statement: Shariful Islam of Tangail went to Saudi Arabia in October 2023 at a cost of BDT 5 lakh, worked for 22 days, was then detained by police and was sent back to Bangladesh in December on an outpass. He says he does not know why he was sent back, does not know whether he paid any insurance money when leaving, has not applied anywhere since returning and nobody told him to.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Islam, returnee from Tangail

facts.statement: Sima of Madaripur, who went to Kuwait to work as an aya at a school leaving three small children with her mother, died there in a road accident. Her mother Manju Begum, who did not know about the insurance, received BDT 35,000 at the airport when the body arrived, later BDT 3 lakh, and after that BDT 10 lakh as insurance compensation.
facts.source_in_article: Manju Begum, mother of the deceased

facts.statement: Amirun Begum of Narsingdi went to Saudi Arabia in November 2022; the death certificate sent from there says she died by suicide on 4 September 2023, and her body reached Bangladesh two months after the death.
facts.source_in_article: her father Harunur Rashid

facts.statement: On 14 January 2024 Harunur Rashid of Narsingdi came to Probashi Kallyan Bhaban in Dhaka to ask when he would get the BDT 3 lakh due for his daughter Amirun Begum's death. In front of the reporter a person working there looked at the death certificate and said, 'Oh, the daughter committed suicide, so she won't get the insurance money.'
facts.source_in_article: reporter's own observation at Probashi Kallyan Bhaban

facts.statement: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP), said that when the destination country writes 'suicide' on the death certificate the worker's family can do nothing more; demands have been raised to bring deaths by suicide and from AIDS or related diseases under the insurance and to give workers health insurance. The article says these demands have been under discussion but not resolved.
facts.source_in_article: Shakirul Islam, chairperson, OKUP

facts.statement: A study by the private research body RMMRU done in 2023 found that 31 percent of women migrant workers' unnatural deaths abroad are from accidents and suicide.
facts.source_in_article: RMMRU study

facts.statement: Professor Tasneem Siddiqui, chair of Dhaka University's political science department and founding chair of RMMRU, said bringing workers under insurance for early return and other reasons, not just death, is very good, but if workers are not told about it the insurance will not be of use.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, RMMRU

headline_en: What a grim example of the rule of law!
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial asks why about 95 percent of cases under the human trafficking prevention law end in acquittal. Citing a home ministry report for January to September 2023 (332 cases, accused acquitted in 316), it blames poor investigation, paid out-of-court settlements and police taking money from both sides. It calls for field-level awareness, accountability for investigators, and notes the government's own report that the high cost of going abroad through official channels pushes people to brokers.

facts.statement: A Ministry of Home Affairs report on human trafficking for January to September 2023 says 332 cases were filed in that period and the accused were acquitted in 316 of them; the editorial describes this as 95 percent of cases under the Prevention of Human Trafficking law being dismissed.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Home Affairs report, as reported by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In 2021-2022 the accused were not convicted in a single human trafficking case in Bangladesh, the editorial says.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing its own report

facts.statement: Stakeholders say accused in trafficking cases are being acquitted because cases are not investigated properly and because of compromise settlements with trafficking rings in exchange for money.
facts.source_in_article: stakeholders quoted in Prothom Alo's report

facts.statement: Salma Ali, president of the Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers' Association, said human trafficking cases are very profitable for police: investigating officers take money from both victims and accused and hold up the investigation for a long time, and members of trafficking rings are highly influential, so the accused are not punished.
facts.source_in_article: Salma Ali, president, Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers' Association

facts.statement: The Ministry of Home Affairs said it has issued investigation guidelines because trafficking cases are being dismissed wholesale; the editorial asks that investigators who do not follow them be held accountable.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Home Affairs, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: The United States' 2023 Trafficking in Persons report said Bangladesh did not meet the minimum standards for preventing human trafficking but is making efforts, and that the capacity of tribunals, legal action and the involvement of law enforcement members need to increase.
facts.source_in_article: US 2023 human trafficking report, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: In 2023 the government, together with the United Nations, published the 'National Study on Trafficking in Persons'.
facts.source_in_article: editorial

facts.statement: The government's own report says trafficking happens more in areas with economic crisis and climate change risk, and that because the cost of going abroad through official channels is high, people fall into brokers' hands and get trafficked.
facts.source_in_article: government report, cited in the editorial

facts.statement: The editorial cites a case of trafficking and rape of a woman in which trial and sentence were completed in India while the same case has been pending in Bangladesh for three years; in another case the trafficked woman is serving jail time in India and her father, who complained against the traffickers, is in jail in a false case while the traffickers were acquitted.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: The editorial says aspiring migrants should be made aware at field level that going abroad illegally through brokers may mean spending the rest of their life in jail.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

headline_en: Claim that the Japanese government will take 100,000 workers a year from Bangladesh is not true
summary_en: A fact-check finds no agreement under which Japan will take one lakh Bangladeshi workers every year for five years, a claim that spread on Facebook and X after Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on 27 October 2026. Japan's foreign ministry spokesperson denied it; the joint statement speaks of Japanese investment creating two lakh jobs inside Bangladesh. A separate employment and skills cooperation memorandum signed on 17 October 2026 has no numerical target, and the 'one lakh' figure traces to a May 2025 report about a five-year target.

facts.statement: There is no agreement between Bangladesh and the Japanese government for Japan to take one lakh workers from Bangladesh each year; the claim that an agreement was signed giving one lakh Bangladeshis a year the chance to go to Japan for the next five years is false.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo fact-check

facts.statement: Kitamura Toshihiro, press secretary and director general for press and public diplomacy of Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a post on X on 29 October 2026 that social media claims that the Japanese government agreed to take one lakh workers from Bangladesh are false and have no truth, and that no such decision or agreement was made at the Japan-Bangladesh summit of 27 October.

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Japan signed the 'Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development' (ESDP-MoC) on 17 October 2026.

facts.statement: Several media outlets reported on 19 October 2026 that under the ESDP-MoC Japan would start recruiting Bangladeshi workers from 1 April of the following year (2027).

facts.statement: The ESDP-MoC with Japan has an initial term of five years and extends automatically for another five years, for an overall term of 10 years; it speaks of ensuring protection of Bangladeshi workers, strengthening cooperation in sending and receiving workers, and creating skill-development opportunities through employment. headline_en: Why Bangladesh's workers are at the centre of the discussion in the Saudi-Houthi war
summary_en: A column by Professor A K M Ahsan Ullah on the October 2026 Houthi-Saudi conflict explains its background and what it could mean for Bangladesh, for which Saudi Arabia is a critical labour market. He warns that a long conflict could cut new hiring, slow construction projects and make wages and overtime uncertain, especially for workers who borrowed to go, and that domestic workers and those at isolated sites may be hard to reach. He urges sector- and region-based preparation: updated embassy contact with workers, wage-recovery arrangements, repatriation if needed, reintegration and alternative markets.

facts.statement: A Houthi-Saudi conflict flared in October 2026; the column refers to attacks on Saudi oil installations and to reports that Aramco quickly restored operations after a recent attack.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: A published report quoting a BMET official's figures said more than seven and a half lakh Bangladeshis went to Saudi Arabia for work in 2025.

facts.statement: The columnist warns that if the Saudi-Houthi conflict is prolonged, new recruitment may fall, construction projects may slow, and wages and overtime income may become uncertain; for a worker who went on loans even a few months without income is a major disaster.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

facts.statement: The columnist says it may be hard to get safety information and help to domestic workers and to workers at isolated workplaces in Saudi Arabia during the conflict.

facts.statement: The columnist says not all sectors will shrink equally: there may still be demand for labour in repair, health care, transport or emergency supply, so Bangladesh's preparation should be sector- and region-based rather than panic-based.

facts.statement: The columnist recommends that Bangladesh plan together for up-to-date embassy contact with workers, a system for recovering unpaid wages, repatriation where necessary, rehabilitation of returning workers, and real investment in alternative labour markets and skills, because over-dependence on one country is safe neither for a family nor for the state.

facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr A K M Ahsan Ullah

headline_en: 'They hand you a weapon and say you won't have to fight, just go forward and back'
summary_en: Thirty Bangladeshis who went to Russia together as construction workers on 7 May 2026 did not get the promised jobs and were sent by deception to fight for Russia; Prothom Alo spoke with 15 of them or their families. At least 20 have died, six are still at the front, two fled hospital and returned home, and two wounded men, Ali Hasan Sohel in Penza and Palash Sheikh in Moscow, are in hospital pleading to be brought back. Bodies of those killed do not come back and families get no compensation; the embassy in Moscow says the two have not contacted it.

facts.statement: Thirty Bangladeshis went to Russia together on 7 May 2026 as construction workers; their families say they did not get the promised jobs in Russia and were sent by deception to fight in the war on Russia's side.
facts.source_in_article: families of the men; Prothom Alo spoke with 15 of the 30

facts.statement: Of the 30 Bangladeshis who went to Russia on 7 May 2026, at least 20 have died, six are still on the battlefield, two escaped from hospital and returned to Bangladesh, and the remaining two are in two different hospitals pleading to return home.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo's own finding from families and the injured

facts.statement: Workers started going from Bangladesh to Russia in 2023 and the flow has multiplied several times over three years; many of them end up in the war, mainly as 'bait', and some die. The exact number is not known, but Prothom Alo has obtained information on the deaths of at least 54 people.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo's own finding

facts.statement: Families of the dead and the injured say the 30 men were taken to an army camp and split into three groups, one of 16. Ali Hasan Sohel says that after only five days of training, five men were sent to the battlefield on the sixth day; they walked mile after mile for three days eating the dry food they carried and reached a tunnel that was an underground army camp, where the other 11 of his group later joined them.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel and families of the dead

facts.statement: Ali Hasan Sohel says men who refuse to fight are confined, beaten and punished until they are forced to go; they are handed a weapon and told they will not have to fight, only move forward and back, right and left. He calls this bait and a death trap: whoever goes is hit by Ukrainian drone attacks; some die and the injured who make it back are taken to hospital for treatment.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel, by video call from hospital in Penza

facts.statement: Ali Hasan Sohel says they were given weapons, dressed in army uniform and sent forward one at a time; of his group of 16, 14 are now missing and the other two are in hospital.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel

facts.statement: Md. Ali Hasan Sohel of Goalanda upazila, Rajbari, has been under treatment for 1 month 10 days at a hospital in Penza, Russia, about 700 km from Moscow; he said he does not know if he will be able to stand on his feet within a year. He said he contacted the Bangladesh embassy, which told him it would try to bring him home when he recovers, but he fears he will be sent back to the war once well.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Hasan Sohel, video call with Prothom Alo on Wednesday 21 October 2026

facts.statement: Md. Palash Sheikh of Gopalganj Sadar upazila, who was in the first group of five sent to the front with Ali Hasan, lost one hand in a drone attack and has been in a Moscow hospital for 24 days. His cousin Abu Saleh Islam said the embassy also said it would try to return him when he recovers, and that Palash wants to return by any means.
facts.source_in_article: Abu Saleh Islam, cousin of Palash Sheikh

facts.statement: Ali Hasan's wife Aklima Khatun applied to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare on 26 July 2026 asking for his rescue and financial help for the family, saying he was cheated and fell into the hands of the Russian army and that the family is under pressure from creditors over loan instalments. Palash Sheikh's sister Chumki Khanam sent a letter to the same ministry on 26 July 2026 asking for diplomatic steps to rescue him and financial help, saying he went to Russia on 7 May on borrowed money and high-interest loans and was handed to the army by force and trickery.
facts.source_in_article: the applications, as described by the reporter

facts.statement: A responsible official of the Bangladesh embassy in Moscow told Prothom Alo that nobody who was injured in the war, is in hospital and wants to return home has yet contacted the embassy about being returned; this contradicts what Ali Hasan and Palash's cousin said about contacting the embassy.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed official, Bangladesh embassy in Moscow

facts.statement: The bodies of Bangladeshis killed in Russia do not come back to Bangladesh, and the families get no compensation.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

facts.statement: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU, said the Bangladesh embassy must contact the Russian government and take responsibility for the two hospitalised men, recover all their treatment costs, dues and compensation from Russia, and arrange their return as soon as they recover.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair, RMMRU

facts.statement: Prothom Alo asked the Russian embassy in Dhaka by email on 21 October 2026 for comment on Bangladeshis being sent to war after being promised work in Russia; no reply is reported in the article.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

headline_en: BDT 1,000 crore in loans for skill development of workers going abroad; how to get up to BDT 10 lakh
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank has launched a BDT 1,000 crore special pre-finance scheme, disbursed through Probashi Kallyan Bank, for skill and language training of Bangladeshis going abroad for work. A worker can borrow up to BDT 10 lakh without collateral at up to 9 percent interest, with two guarantors. The article sets out eligibility, what the loan covers, required documents and the online application process; by 4 October 2026, 481 people had received BDT 13.03 crore.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank launched a BDT 1,000 crore special pre-finance scheme to support skill development and language learning for Bangladeshis going abroad for employment; the fund is given through Probashi Kallyan Bank, and workers going abroad can take a collateral-free loan of up to BDT 10 lakh from it.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank; reporter

facts.statement: The BDT 1,000 crore fund will be given to Probashi Kallyan Bank in five equal instalments of BDT 200 crore; the next instalment is released only after checking that the previous one was properly used.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Salahuddin Tafadar, additional director, Bangladesh Bank, in a podcast on Bangladesh Bank's Facebook page

facts.statement: The loan carries a maximum interest of 9 percent. The initial term is three years including a six-month grace period, and the term can be extended to five years if needed.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: One person can borrow a maximum of BDT 10 lakh under the scheme. No collateral is needed, but two guarantors are required: one a close family member and the other a person established in society and able to repay the loan.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: The loan covers the tuition fee for language or job-skill training taken in the destination country after going abroad and, in specified cases, living and food costs; the air ticket is not covered.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: Bangladeshis who want to go abroad legally for employment can apply for the loan; students going abroad to study are not eligible.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank scheme terms, as reported

facts.statement: Probashi Kallyan Bank managing director Wahida Begum said Bangladeshis going abroad for employment through any legal channel, government or private, can get a loan under the bank's migration loan policy.
facts.source_in_article: Wahida Begum, managing director, Probashi Kallyan Bank

facts.statement: Documents needed for the loan: valid passport, visa, the required Certificate of Eligibility, and a certificate of qualification for the language or skill training; an offer letter from the training or educational institution is important and must state the tuition fee, how many months it is needed for, and who will bear living and food costs.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

facts.statement: The loan application is made through Probashi Kallyan Bank's website, with no need to visit a branch to apply, and the applicant can track progress online. The information and papers are first verified at branch level, then sent to the bank's head office; if approved, an approval letter is sent to the branch, and after final approval the applicant must go to the branch in person to give consent to take the loan.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

facts.statement: According to Probashi Kallyan Bank, BDT 13.03 crore had been disbursed to 481 people under the scheme up to 4 October 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Probashi Kallyan Bank

facts.statement: A two-tier monitoring system is in place so the loan money is used for its set purpose; Bangladesh Bank's SME and Special Programmes Department oversees the fund.
facts.source_in_article: reporter

headline_en: Arabic is the 'language of remittance', so why is it so neglected in training?
summary_en: A column argues that Arabic should be a core part of training for workers going to the Middle East, since language protects workers from fraud, wage theft and harassment. It notes the three-day pre-departure orientation cannot teach a language, and that Arabic instructors appointed at 32 TTCs have no clear policy on their duties or future. The writer proposes a separate Arabic trade with one- to three-month courses, compulsory for certain occupations and visas.

facts.statement: According to Bangladesh Bank, a record USD 35.59 billion in remittance came to Bangladesh in FY2025-26, about 60 percent of it from the oil-rich Middle East countries; Saudi Arabia alone sent USD 5.85 billion and the United Arab Emirates USD 4.58 billion.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank data, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Workers going to the Middle East currently have a three-day pre-departure orientation (PDO) training; the columnist says basic skill in a language cannot be gained in three days.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

facts.statement: Arabic language instructors have been appointed at 32 TTCs (technical training centres) in Bangladesh, but there is no clear policy on their duties and future: sometimes they are told to teach Arabic, sometimes to take classes of other trades, and there are rumours they may be dropped.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

facts.statement: The columnist says a worker who knows the language can speak about their rights, understand the employer's instructions, ask about the contract and explain their situation in danger; without it they depend on others, which exposes them to fraud, wage deprivation, workplace discrimination and harassment.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

facts.statement: The columnist proposes a separate Arabic trade at TTCs, a one- to three-month basic Arabic course for Middle East-bound workers, making it compulsory for certain occupations and visas, testing language skill after training, a permanent policy and job structure for the instructors, and coordination among BMET, the expatriates' welfare ministry and the TTCs. facts.source_in_article: columnist Mufti Maulana Shaikh Muhammad Usman Gani

headline_en: Bangladeshi student killed in Cyprus; ransom was still being demanded after he was buried
summary_en: Shahriar Ahmed alias Emon (22) of Raipura, Narsingdi, who went to Cyprus on a student visa three months earlier, went missing on 11 June 2026 after going out to start a night-shift job in Larnaca; police recovered his buried, decomposed body on Sunday 21 June 2026 in the Kofinou area. From the night he vanished, unknown persons used his WhatsApp to demand a ransom of 35,000 euros from his father. Cyprus police arrested a Bangladeshi, Shahin Babu (22), who relatives say confessed and led police to the body and knife.

facts.statement: Shahriar Ahmed alias Emon (22), a Bangladeshi student living in the Oroklini area of Larnaca, Cyprus, went missing after 9 pm on 11 June 2026 when he went out to join a job; on Sunday 21 June 2026 Cyprus police recovered his decomposed body buried at a place in the Kofinou area of Larnaca. Relatives quoting Cyprus police say he was stabbed to death the night he went missing and then buried.
facts.source_in_article: relatives, quoting Cyprus police

facts.statement: On the afternoon of 11 June 2026 Shahriar told his mother a job had been arranged for him, night duty, starting that night; at 9 pm local time he reached the work location and sent the location on WhatsApp to his roommate Raihan Mia. Around 10 pm a message came from Shahriar's own WhatsApp number to his father saying he had been kidnapped, demanding 35,000 euros, and threatening to remove and sell his eyes and kidneys if it was not paid.
facts.source_in_article: family members

facts.statement: Unknown persons used Shahriar's phone and WhatsApp number to demand a ransom of 35,000 euros (printed as BDT 50 lakh) from his father Nasir Mia, from the night he disappeared until just before the body was found; the number stayed online 24 hours and money was demanded daily. The family bargained the demand down to BDT 5 lakh and went to a bank on Sunday afternoon to send it, but did not pay because the callers refused to let them speak to Shahriar even once.
facts.source_in_article: Nayan Ahmed, brother of the deceased

facts.statement: Cyprus police on Sunday 21 June 2026 arrested a Bangladeshi youth named Shahin Babu (22) on the charge of involvement in the killing; relatives quoting police say Shahriar's phone was recovered from him, he confessed during questioning, and his information led police to the buried body and the knife used. Police did not confirm where in Bangladesh Shahin Babu is from.
facts.source_in_article: relatives, quoting Cyprus police

facts.statement: When Shahriar did not return from work the next morning, his roommate Raihan Mia went to the police station and reported it; going with police to the location Shahriar had sent did not find him.
facts.source_in_article: family members

facts.statement: Shahriar went to Cyprus on a student visa about three months before his death, near the end of Ramadan, having been admitted online to a university there while still in Bangladesh; his family had to send BDT 40,000 to 50,000 a month for his expenses, and he was trying to find a job so he would not need money from home.
facts.source_in_article: family members

facts.statement: Raipura Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md. Masud Rana said he had heard of the body's recovery but had not been officially informed by the embassy and the family had not contacted his office; if they ask for help, necessary steps will be taken through the ministry. The mother, Papia Begum, asked for justice and for the body to be brought home.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Masud Rana, UNO, Raipura; Papia Begum

headline_en: Focus on advancing cooperation in various sectors
summary_en: After a bilateral meeting in Putrajaya on Monday 22 June 2026, Prime Ministers Tarique Rahman and Anwar Ibrahim issued a joint statement covering labour recruitment, trade and investment, energy, semiconductors and defence. On labour, the two sides decided to call a Joint Working Group meeting so that a new memorandum of understanding on worker recruitment can be drafted. Tarique Rahman said he asked Malaysia to hire more Bangladeshi workers, open the labour market quickly, regularise irregular workers and consider repatriating detained Bangladeshis.

headline_en: Tarique Rahman meets Anwar Ibrahim today; what will get priority alongside the labour market

Besides trade, energy and education, the labour market is a main topic: Malaysia has been the second main destination for new Bangladeshi workers after Saudi Arabia for a decade, but its New Industrial Master Plan 2030 is shrinking the market for the kind of workers Bangladesh sends. headline_en: Why 'virtual migration' is a new opportunity for Bangladesh
summary_en: A column by Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder of North South University argues that 'virtual migration', working for foreign employers online while staying in Bangladesh, is a timely alternative to physical labour migration, which wars and instability in the Middle East and Ukraine have made less safe. He distinguishes it from freelancing and outsourcing, cites India, the Philippines and Romania, lists jobs learnable in 3 to 6 months, and names returnee migrants and migrant families among target groups. He notes it has no formal recognition, labour law, protection or reliable statistics in Bangladesh and calls for coordination across ministries.

facts.statement: The columnist says the Iran-Israel tension, the Ukraine war and instability in the Middle East mean going abroad to work is no longer as safe or assured as before, a major risk for a country dependent on foreign labour markets because the political or military situation can change at any time.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist defines 'virtual migration' as a worker staying in their own country while working directly for a foreign organisation, in many cases as a regular employee and without an intermediary organisation; he distinguishes it from freelancing (individual, short-term, project-based, uncertain work with no fixed employer) and outsourcing (work transferred from one company to another, with workers under a local firm).
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: The columnist says work open to young Bangladeshis through virtual migration includes graphic design, video editing, data entry, virtual customer service, online tutoring, medical support, accounting and IT support, and that a person can be job-ready after 3 to 6 months of training: 3 months for data entry or customer service, 4 months for graphic design or digital marketing, 6 months for web development, accounting or IT support.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: The columnist names rural youth, women, returnee migrants, unemployed graduates and members of migrant families as the groups best suited for virtual migration with short-term training.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: Virtual migration has not yet received formal recognition in Bangladesh, and there is no labour law, protection or reliable statistics for it; the ICT ministry works on digital skills and the expatriates' welfare ministry on sending workers abroad, but the two operate separately. The columnist calls for an 'under one umbrella' framework involving the ICT, expatriates' welfare, education and labour ministries.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder

facts.statement: Research by Otto Kassi and Vili Lehdonvirta ('How many online workers are there in the world') found about 163 million people registered on online labour platforms worldwide, of whom about 19 million have actually obtained work and at least 5 million earn significant income.
facts.source_in_article: Kassi and Lehdonvirta study, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: In the Philippines more than 1.5 million people are engaged in online or remote work and the IT-BPO sector earns about USD 38 billion a year (citing The Philippine Star, 16 January 2025); the columnist says women who earlier went abroad in large numbers as domestic workers now work from home as virtual assistants and in customer support, reducing the need for risky migration.
facts.source_in_article: columnist, citing The Philippine Star, 16 January 2025

facts.statement: A Romania Journal report of 8 January 2026 says 12 to 15 percent of workers in Romania now work remotely or in hybrid mode, against under 5 percent before Covid.
facts.source_in_article: Romania Journal, 8 January 2026, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: A study by Sanjay Sugandhi and Shrikant Tare ('Work from home: a revolution in Indian scenario') found about 12.7 percent of workers in India work fully from home and another 28.2 percent in hybrid mode.
facts.source_in_article: Sugandhi and Tare study, cited by the columnist
